common_name: Little Scarlet Alpine Strawberry (Heritage English Jam Strawberry)

planting.note: Surface-sow the dust-fine seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and keep evenly moist, since this old English market strain germinates slowly and unevenly.

directions: Little Scarlet is a diminutive, intensely flavored English strain long grown commercially in Norfolk hedgerows for its deep red, aromatic fruit used in traditional whole-fruit preserves rather than fresh eating. The small, tightly held berries ripen over a long summer season and resist the bland wateriness common in larger modern fruit. Plants tolerate dappled shade from hedges or taller companions better than conventional June-bearing strawberries, making them a good fit for the edge of a woodland or shade food garden. Divide congested clumps every two to three years to maintain vigor and fruit size.

common_name: Golden Alexandria Alpine Strawberry (Gold-Variegated Woodland Strawberry)

planting.note: Start seed indoors on the soil surface 8-10 weeks before last frost; grow on under bright light since variegated seedlings are slower to establish than plain green forms.

directions: Golden Alexandria is a gold-splashed sport of the everbearing Alexandria alpine strawberry, grown as much for its bright, mottled foliage as for its small, sweet red fruit. The variegation is most vivid in cooler weather and light shade, and plants can scorch or revert toward plain green if pushed into hot, full sun. Use it as an edible edging or underplanting in a shaded border where its foliage color carries visual interest between the light but steady summer-into-fall fruit set. Remove any all-green reverted shoots promptly to keep the clump true to its variegated form.
sources: Plant World Seeds (Devon, UK) variety descriptions

planting.note: Set divisions or nursery plugs out around last frost into humus-rich soil; this cultivar is most often propagated by division since variegation does not always come true from seed.

directions: Variegata is a cream-and-green marbled-leaf form of the European wild strawberry, grown primarily as a low ornamental groundcover that happens to produce small, edible red fruit. Its patterned foliage brightens shaded walkways and woodland-edge plantings, and it tends to stay more compact than plain-leaf alpine strawberries. Because variegated leaf tissue photosynthesizes less efficiently, give it reliably moist, humus-rich soil and expect a lighter fruit set than from solid-green cultivars. Divide and replant crowded patches every few years to keep the variegation strong and prevent the center of the clump from thinning out.

common_name: Monophylla One-Leaf Alpine Strawberry (Single-Leaflet Woodland Strawberry)

planting.note: Surface-sow indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; this curiosity strain breeds reasonably true from seed collected off isolated plants.

directions: Monophylla is a long-collected botanical curiosity of the wild strawberry in which each leaf is reduced to a single rounded leaflet instead of the usual three, giving the plant a distinctive, almost clover-free texture in a shaded border. It fruits and spreads much like any alpine strawberry, producing small aromatic red berries over a long season, and is grown by collectors chiefly for its unusual foliage rather than for heavy cropping. Partial shade and consistently moist, well-drained soil keep the clump healthy and slow its tendency to seed back toward the normal three-leaflet form. Remove any seedlings or runners that revert to typical foliage if you want to maintain a pure single-leaflet patch.

planting.note: Surface-sow indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; keep seedlings in bright, indirect light since this heirloom strain is slower and less vigorous than typical alpine strawberries.

directions: The Plymouth strawberry is a centuries-old English curiosity in which the carpels on the fruit surface are enlarged into small leafy, hose-in-hose structures rather than lying flat as ordinary seeds, giving each berry a shaggy, spiny-looking texture. It was recorded in English gardens as early as the seventeenth century and is grown today mainly by heirloom collectors and botanic gardens rather than for its modest, often sparse crop. Grow it like other woodland strawberries in humus-rich soil with light shade, where its novelty fruit and typical trifoliate leaves make an interesting talking point along a shaded path. Because seedlings can revert to normal fruit form, save seed only from plants showing the characteristic hose-in-hose berries.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society historical plant records
